lesson.title: The Safe Base: What Secure Attachment Looks Like
lesson.summary: Secure attachment is the pattern in which infants use their caregiver as a safe base for exploration and are readily comforted by them after distress, and it is associated with generally positive outcomes for social and emotional development.
lesson.body:
Secure attachment is the attachment style most infants show in Ainsworth's Strange Situation, and it is generally treated as the pattern associated with healthy early social and emotional development. A securely attached infant uses their caregiver as what researchers call a secure base: while the caregiver is present, the infant feels free to explore the unfamiliar room and interact with new toys or even the stranger, periodically checking back or glancing toward the caregiver. When the caregiver leaves, the infant typically shows some distress, which is a normal and expected part of the pattern rather than a sign of insecurity on its own. What distinguishes secure attachment is what happens at reunion: when the caregiver returns, the securely attached infant actively seeks comfort from them, whether through reaching to be picked up or simply moving closer, is readily soothed, and then returns fairly quickly to playing and exploring.

This pattern is generally thought to develop from a caregiving history in which the caregiver has been reasonably consistent and responsive to the infant's needs and signals over time, sensitive enough that the infant has learned, through repeated experience, that the caregiver is a reliable source of comfort when needed. This directly reflects the internal working model idea from attachment theory: consistent, responsive caregiving appears to build an expectation that others can generally be trusted and relied upon in moments of need.

Secure attachment in infancy is associated with a range of generally positive outcomes later in childhood, including better emotion regulation, more positive peer relationships, and greater resilience when facing stress, and some research follows these associations into adolescence and adulthood as well. It is important to be careful about the strength of this claim, though: these are correlational associations built up across decades of research, not guarantees for any individual child, and many other factors, including temperament, later relationships, and the broader environment a child grows up in, continue to shape development well beyond infancy. Attachment style in infancy is a meaningful early influence, not a fixed, unchangeable verdict on how a person's relationships will turn out for the rest of their life.
